title: Fats, Oils, and Grease (FOG) in Sink Drain Traps
description: An educational breakdown explaining how liquid cooking fats cool and congeal inside a sink P-trap, gradually restricting drainage flow.
image_prompt: A professional 9:16 vertical educational technical cutaway diagram of a kitchen sink drainage assembly under a residential countertop. High resolution, photo-realistic textures. The visual clearly shows a stainless steel sink bowl at the top connecting down through a vertical tailpiece into a white PVC tubular P-trap. A clean, cross-sectional cutaway reveals the interior of the P-trap. Inside the lower bend of the trap, a thick layer of solidified, yellowish congealed grease and trapped food particles coat the inner pipe wall, significantly restricting the water channel. Clear water is visible above the blockage, demonstrating restricted flow. Crisp indoor workshop ambient lighting, clean background, focus centered on the cutaway P-trap fitting. Physically accurate pipe wall thickness and slip-nut connections. No text, no logos, no watermarks, no annotations, no arrows, vertical 9:16 ratio.
visual_story: The visual directs attention to the internal dip of a kitchen P-trap using a longitudinal sectional cutaway. Viewers observe how liquid fats do not stay fluid; upon reaching the cooler standing water inside the trap, they solidify along the pipe walls. This visual clearly demonstrates the exact mechanism of a FOG buildup, helping the viewer understand why liquid grease creates hard blockages over time.

on_image_text.hook: Why Liquid Cooking Grease Blocks Sink Drains
on_image_text.explanation: Warm fats liquefy when cooking, but rapidly solidify when contacting the cold water seal in the trap.
on_image_text.callout: Congealed FOG layer narrowing internal pipe diameter
on_image_text.takeaway: Wipe pans with paper towels into the trash before washing to keep traps clear.
